name: Leanmaxxing

lead: Leanmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for lowering body fat so the jawline and cheekbones show and the face looks sharper. It is often the first step people take.

Losing body fat reduces facial fullness, which is widely observed, revealing the bone structure underneath. It is essentially a cutting phase, and the specific body-fat levels cited on forums come from anecdote; no published studies on facial leanness and attractiveness were found in the sources examined.

paras: People estimate maintenance calories, track intake and eat below it, adding cardio or lifting. Megathreads on looksmax.org offer calculators, tips and progress reports. Users discuss that going below roughly 15 percent body fat gets harder, and some mention appetite-control drugs or supplements.
Aggressive deficits can lead to muscle loss, low energy and hormonal effects, and posters include teenagers. Drug-assisted fat loss mentioned in forums carries the risks of those substances.

angle.text: Leanmaxxing is often the first step in looksmaxxing: lose body fat to reveal cheekbones and the jawline. Fat loss reducing facial fullness is widely observed; the exact body-fat levels cited on forums come from anecdote.

lead: Leanmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for lowering body fat in order to make the face and body look more defined. The idea is that a thinner face shows the jawline, cheekbones and under-eye area more clearly, and that a leaner body makes the neck, shoulders and waist look more athletic. Forum members frequently describe it as the first and most accessible step in an appearance overhaul, because it needs no procedure or product beyond changes to eating and activity.[1][2][3]

In practice it is a cutting phase: people estimate how many calories they burn, track what they eat, and eat below that level for weeks or months, usually adding resistance training and cardio. One long-running looksmax.org megathread directs readers to body-fat and energy-expenditure calculators, food-tracking apps and a deficit below estimated maintenance.[2] Other threads offer motivational posts, shortcuts, progress photos and numbered fat-loss guides.[1][4][5][6][7]

Research on the face and body fat is real, although it was not designed around looksmaxxing. Studies of facial adiposity find that observers can estimate a person's body mass index from a face, and that facial fatness is associated with ratings of attractiveness and health in several samples.[8][8][9] Other work notes that facial cues to health are mixed across studies.[8] Weight-loss science, covered by general references, describes fat loss as the product of a sustained energy deficit, with resistance training suggested to preserve muscle.[10]

The topic also attracts discussion of faster routes, including GLP-1 medicines originally developed for diabetes and obesity, and of very low body-fat targets. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists extreme dieting and unregulated GLP-1 use among the harder-edged practices in the wider scene, and sports-medicine and psychiatry sources describe the health issues associated with chronic low energy availability and with body-image disorders.[3][11][12][13]

paras: Leanmaxxing refers to reducing body fat to improve appearance, with particular attention to facial definition.[1][14] On looksmax.org it appears as a recurring thread title, with motivational posts, tip lists, guides and progress updates under the label.[1][4][5][15] One motivation thread became a chant of the phrase "get lean or get left behind" in its replies, which shows how members frame leanness as a baseline expectation.[1]

Wikipedia describes looksmaxxing as an online self-improvement practice aimed at male attractiveness, divided into softmaxxing (skincare, grooming, clothing, fitness and weight management) and hardmaxxing (more extreme measures, including dieting to very low body fat, off-label drugs and surgery).[3] Leanmaxxing sits mainly in the softmaxxing half, with the harder-edged variants appearing at its extremes.

Face. Posters talk about the jawline, cheekbone shadows and hollower cheeks, the so-called bones that appear as facial fat drops.[15] Anatomy sources describe the buccal fat pad as a deep fat mass in the cheek that is involved in the formation of hollow cheeks, and some people discuss it when explaining why some faces change more than others.[16]
Neck and body. Another thread treats neck size as part of the same project, and the debates about lean versus muscular physiques extend the focus from the face to overall build.[14][17]

Perception. Facial shape carries information about body weight. A 2017 study of 272 faces from Malaysian Chinese, UK Caucasian and black South African participants built models predicting body mass index, body fat and blood pressure from facial shape, and found that when participants adjusted faces to look as healthy as possible they lowered the predicted BMI and body fat.[9]

Community guides describe the general method: estimate body fat percentage with a tape-based formula, estimate daily energy expenditure, track food intake with an app, and eat below maintenance. The megathread lists several calculators and tracking apps and mentions lean protein and vegetables as staples.[2] Other threads describe strategies in numbered guides and shortcuts for reducing effort.[6][7]

General references describe the same mechanism. Weight loss occurs when energy expenditure exceeds intake, and the weight lost can include fluid, fat and lean mass. Logging food regularly is associated with larger losses, and weight training is recommended to preserve or build muscle.[10] The Wikipedia article on body fat percentage lists calipers, bioelectrical impedance, DXA and circumference formulas as measurement methods, and notes that BMI alone cannot give an accurate body fat estimate.[18]

Members discuss whether to carry on cutting, how long to run a deficit, and what to do when progress slows. Thread titles include requests for advice on continuing a cut and progress updates reporting that someone is not there yet.[19]

A recurring debate compares a light, very lean person with a heavier, stronger one, for example a thread asking which of two men of equal height would be seen as better looking.[14] Bodybuilding sources describe cutting as eating below maintenance to lose fat while retaining muscle, with larger deficits raising the risk of muscle loss.[19]

Members also post about how hard progress becomes below roughly 15 percent body fat.[20] Reference material notes that the lowest body-fat levels are reached by athletes and bodybuilders for short periods and that measurement at the low end is less reliable.[18]

sections.h: Research on facial fat, attractiveness and health
paras: A 2018 review in Frontiers in Psychology on facial adiposity, attractiveness and health included a meta-analysis of studies relating perceived facial adiposity to BMI or body fat; it reported that people could estimate BMI from facial cues alone with a summary correlation of 0.71, and linked facial adiposity to attractiveness and health judgments.[8]

A cross-sectional study of 162 young men, with faces rated by eight women, measured body fat by skinfold and reported that skinfold thickness and poor health symptoms negatively predicted attractiveness ratings.[8] A 2025 study of 105 healthy men found that attractiveness and masculinity ratings were negatively linked to adiposity and positively linked to testosterone.[8] A 2020 study combined ratings and EEG recordings for morphed female faces at five levels of body fat percentage in 40 young adults.[8]

The research literature also contains cautions. A 2025 scoping review of 21 studies found mixed results on whether facial features act as honest indicators of health.[8] The 2017 shape study found that predicted BMI and blood pressure correlated with health ratings while predicted body fat did not.[9] Wikipedia's facial attractiveness article also records work on body composition, including a 2016 study of Australian university students in which the male body composition rated most attractive fell within a healthy range.[21]
No published study has tested leanmaxxing as a programme, or its effect on how a particular person's face is rated before and after fat loss.

Some looksmax.org posts discuss using appetite-reducing products. One thread is a field report combining semaglutide, a branded fibre product and glucomannan.[22] Semaglutide is a prescription medicine; the US FDA approved Ozempic for type 2 diabetes in December 2017 and Wegovy for weight management in June 2021.[11] In a 2021 phase III trial of 1,961 adults with obesity, mean weight change was -14.9 percent at 68 weeks on semaglutide against -2.4 percent on placebo.[11]

Reported side effects include nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, constipation and abdominal pain, and gallstones are a noted risk; the US label carries a boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumours based on rodent studies.[11] Wikipedia also records shortages from 2022, compounded versions, and counterfeit pens reported in Europe in 2023, and says people without obesity or diabetes obtain GLP-1 drugs through an unregulated grey market in the looksmaxxing scene.[3][11] This wiki gives no dosing or sourcing information.

Sports-medicine sources describe relative energy deficiency in sport as arising when intake is too low for the energy being spent, with effects on hormones and bone; in men, prolonged low energy availability is reported to reduce androgen levels, and bone mass peaks between about 18 and 25, so deficits in youth may have lasting effects.[12]

Psychiatric sources describe muscle dysmorphia, a body dysmorphic disorder subtype, as involving dietary restriction, overtraining and supplement or drug use, with onset commonly between ages 18 and 20.[13] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article also links the community's rating culture to body dysmorphia and notes extreme dieting to the point of starvation among its harder-edged practices.[3]

Wikipedia's article on the buccal fat pad notes that surgical removal of cheek fat, sometimes done to reduce cheek prominence, can carry a significant risk of damage to the facial nerve branch and parotid ducts.[16]
No studies found on leanmaxxing as a named practice. Related research is described under facial adiposity above; semaglutide has trial data for weight loss in people with obesity.[11][8]

Threads include before-and-after posts, neck-size threads and drug field reports, and a Portuguese-language thread urges members to do it or be left behind.[15][22][17] The topic sits alongside muscle-building and skin threads as part of the standard softmaxxing checklist.[3] Forum humour about the effort required, such as skipping meals all day, appears in replies to the megathread.[2]

lore.intro: Leanmaxxing is regarded in many posts as a basic requirement for a defined face, and the community mixes advice, humour and pressure about it.[1][15]

timeline.event: Pope and colleagues describe muscle dysmorphia as an underrecognised form of body dysmorphic disorder.[13]
The term looksmaxxing is coined on online message boards.[3]
An IOC consensus statement introduces the term relative energy deficiency in sport.[12]
Facial shape analysis study links face shape to BMI and body fat; US approval of Ozempic.[11][9]
Frontiers in Psychology review and meta-analysis relates perceived facial adiposity to BMI.[8]
Wegovy approved in the US for weight management; phase III trial reports about 15 percent mean weight loss.[11]
Media coverage including the New York Times and Business Insider reports looksmaxxing as a TikTok trend.[3]
BBC and The Conversation cover the trend; a Frontiers study links skinfold thickness to rated facial attractiveness.[3][8]
A scoping review of 21 studies finds mixed evidence that facial features signal health.[8]
